newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU compromise seen on delayed Italy, Spain entry.
newsitem.headline: EMU compromise seen on delayed Italy, Spain entry.

text.p: A political compromise for Italy and Spain that would allow them rapid entry into a commmon European currency after it is launched in 1999 is an idea favoured by EU monetary officials and analysts.

While many say that Italy and Spain have relatively slim chances of qualifying on all the Maastricht Treaty requirements for economic and monetary union (EMU), their efforts towards durable economic reform cannot go unrewarded.

For the EU's objective of closer integration, a political signal giving the two countries a ticket into EMU shortly after its start is seen necessary to keep progress alive on several thorny issues like EU enlargement, foreign and defence policy.

"Whether they can join (EMU) in the first wave is still an open question," said one senior EU official. "But I think it's likely they will get a promise they can join if not in the first wave then very shortly after."
The issue of whether Italy can enter EMU on time came to a head this week when French President Jacques Chirac cast doubt on the country's fitness to join the first wave of members.
Chirac infuriated Rome, prompting him to reverse his statement and allow a planned summit between the two nations to go ahead.
The timing of any deal on EMU remains uncertain, but most think it would likely come about in early 1998, when the EU decides which countries qualify for the single currency.

Any earlier move might take the pressure off Italy and Spain to stick to the tough budgetary reforms announced in recent weeks. There is also every incentive to keep alive the option of them joining in the first wave, even though the odds appear against them, officials say.
The idea of delaying EMU's start date is not seen as a viable alternative given the great financial risks involved.
As one official put it: "The stakes of this whole project rises exponentially the closer we get to the start date. To delay it would involve immense damage."

For France and Germany, the problem of how to deal with a country like Italy remains a difficult balancing act. Issues such as competitive currency devaluation and domestic political support for EMU are among their main concerns.
The French have long argued that the Italian lira's depreciation in recent years has harmed their industries by giving Italy an unfair export advantage.

The lira has risen considerably in recent months and now poses a threat to Italy's own export industries. But there is still a perception in France the currency must appreciate further before it can rejoin the European Exchange Rate Mechanism that it dropped out of in 1992.
Germany, which has remained conspicuously silent in the latest Franco-Italian row, is more concerned with public opinion.
Analysts say it is no secret that Bonn would have a tough job in selling EMU to Germans, who remain wedded to the strong mark, if countries like Italy or Spain are included at the start.
Despite the efforts both nations have made in bringing their public finances under control, many Germans still view Italy as having a unreliable currency and political system.

"I think the most likely option is that (the EU) will give them a promise that if they persevere they will be able to join (EMU) at a certain pre-fixed time period," said Daniel Gros, economist at the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels.
